Class ActorNet

java.lang.Object
dev.swordai.core.rl.ActorNet
public final class ActorNet extends Object
The acting network: two small CNNs over the enemy masks and an MLP over the vector input, joined into one trunk that feeds the action heads.

Two keys are not the trunk's. Each has a small model of its own, fed by the vector input only (the fighter's own body, and where and how large the opponent is on screen):

  • the crit model decides the jump key, always. And whenever a critical hit can be in the making (JumpNudge.critMoment(float[]): in a jump of its own from take-off to landing, and coming down after the opponent's hit has knocked it up, which is where a punish crit is made) it also has the sprint key, and W/S unless the escape model has those. The trunk, which is the sprint-hit fighter, has no say in those keys then. A critical hit is not a jump: it is a swing made on the way down with the sprint off, and a fighter that has spent a million steps learning never to let go of the sprint does not let go of it because it has jumped. (0.11.3: forty jumps a minute, nine hits in ten still sprint hits, not one critical.) So in those moments the crit model starts out leaving W alone and the sprint key up, which ends the sprint.

    The swing is the crit model's for as long as the fighter is off the ground at all (JumpNudge.inAir(float[])), so also on the way up after a hit: it starts out swinging when it is coming down with the weapon back and the sprint off, and not before. That is what keeps the swing for the punish crit instead of spending it on the way up. But a swing in the air takes two: the crit model's "now it would be critical", and the trunk's "there is a hit to be had". The trunk has spent its whole training on whether the opponent is under the crosshair and near enough; where it would not swing, the swing is held back (NO_HIT_MOST). Up to 0.12.3 the trunk was not asked, and the fighter swung on the way down of every jump whatever was in front of it: at an opponent out of reach that is a miss, and the weapon is gone for the hit that was to be had a moment later.

  • the escape model decides W/S in the twelve ticks after each hit of a combo the fighter is taking (BackNudge.applies(float[])): the ticks in which it backs out or does not. The rest of the time W/S is the trunk's, as before, and with it coming back in at a sprint for the hit.

Why: both are things the fighter learns late, on keys it has long since settled on never pressing (jump) or always pressing one way (W). Taught inside the one network, the new use either never got started or spread to everywhere (0.9.0 to 0.10.0: it held S all the time). A model of its own starts undecided, so it tries the key from its first tick, and nothing it learns can change what the rest of the network does: its gradient ends in it, and its output is only ever used for its own key in its own moment.

    • oppFilm

    • critTrunk

      private final Dense critTrunk
      What the trunk has made of the fight (what the heads read: after the blocks, the tactic and the reader) into the crit model and the escape model, and the reader's numbers into the crit model; null without Config.critBridge. Until then the two read the vector input alone and never knew which opponent they faced. They start at zero, and nothing they learn goes back into the trunk or the reader, which keep learning exactly as they did.

  • Method Details

    • restAir

      private void restAir()
      How the crit model starts out in the air: no W and no S, and the sprint key up. A hit is only critical if the server does not have the fighter sprinting, and that is what kept critical hits at exactly none for as long as the trunk held the keys: it lets go of W after every hit and presses it again with the sprint key down, which starts the sprint again each time. Letting go of W ends a sprint. Pressing W twice within seven ticks starts one, sprint key or no (the game's double-tap), so W pressed now and then in the air starts it again too, which is what the first version of this (0.12.0) did. With W left alone and the sprint key up, the sprint ends on the first tick in the air and stays ended.

    • calmInitialPolicy

      private static void calmInitialPolicy(float[] bias)
      Biases every head towards "do little": small camera moves, keys up. A head stays at this prior until its stage unlocks it, so a freshly unlocked control explores gently instead of thrashing the camera and wrecking the skills that were learned before it.

    • reopenHead

      public void reopenHead(int head, float restBias)
      Puts one head back to how a head starts: no weight on anything the trunk says, and its default choice ahead of the others by restBias. The optimiser's memory of it is cleared too.
